clinicalPearls: The classic combination is painful pseudodendritic keratitis with palmoplantar keratoderma, often with variable intellectual disability
Autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in TAT, encoding hepatic tyrosine aminotransferase (tyrosinaemia type II)
Ocular symptoms such as photophobia, tearing and redness can precede skin lesions and may be misdiagnosed as herpetic keratitis
Painful hyperkeratotic lesions affect the palms and soles and can be a prominent complaint
Marked hypertyrosinaemia is the biochemical signature, with raised plasma tyrosine and increased urinary tyrosine metabolites
Unlike tyrosinaemia type I, there is no hepatorenal disease; the toxicity is due to tyrosine crystal deposition
Dietary restriction of tyrosine and phenylalanine improves the ocular and cutaneous features and may protect neurodevelopment
Corneal lesions are typically bilateral, which helps distinguish them from infective dendritic ulcers
reference.pathophysiology: Richner-Hanhart syndrome is caused by deficiency of hepatic cytosolic tyrosine aminotransferase, the first enzyme of tyrosine catabolism, due to biallelic TAT variants. The block causes tyrosine to accumulate in blood and tissues. Supersaturated tyrosine crystallises within cells, and the resulting crystalline deposition triggers an inflammatory response in the cornea and skin, producing the characteristic pseudodendritic keratitis and painful palmoplantar keratoderma. Elevated tyrosine may also affect the developing brain, accounting for the variable intellectual disability. Because the disorder does not involve the downstream toxic metabolites of tyrosinaemia type I, the liver and kidneys are spared; lowering tyrosine through dietary restriction of tyrosine and phenylalanine reverses the crystal-driven ocular and skin disease.
additionalDifferentials: Tyrosinaemia type I and type III
Other causes of infantile keratitis or photophobia
additionalInvestigations: Plasma amino acids showing marked hypertyrosinaemia
Urine organic acids for tyrosine metabolites
Slit-lamp examination for bilateral pseudodendritic keratitis
redFlags: Severe or ulcerating keratitis threatening vision
Diagnostic confusion with recurrent herpetic keratitis leading to inappropriate antiviral or steroid use
reference.prognosis: With early dietary restriction of tyrosine and phenylalanine the ocular and skin lesions resolve and neurodevelopmental outcome can be favourable; untreated disease risks corneal scarring and cognitive impairment.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the bilateral pseudodendritic keratitis as herpes simplex and treating accordingly
Overlooking hypertyrosinaemia as the unifying cause of eye and skin findings
Assuming hepatorenal involvement as in tyrosinaemia type I
Delaying dietary treatment and allowing corneal or neurological damage
